column2: How fast should I run?
Effort, talk test and heart rate zones – how to get every session right.
The effort scale (RPE)
The plans often say “RPE 3–4/10”. RPE means: how hard does it feel – 1 is walking, 10 is complete exhaustion.
RPE 2–4: easy. You can speak in full sentences. This is the pace for base, recovery and long runs.
RPE 5–6: brisk. Short sentences are still possible, a conversation gets hard. Typical for tempo runs.
RPE 7–9: hard. Only single words. This is the zone for intervals and hill sprints.
Talk test
The simplest test on the go: say a full sentence out loud. If you can do it without gasping, you're in the easy zone.
If you can no longer talk on an easy run, slow down or walk a few steps – that's not failure, it's training right.
Heart rate zones
Zone 1 (very easy, approx. 50–60% of maximum heart rate): cool-down, recovery.
Zone 2 (easy, approx. 60–70%): most of your training. Builds endurance without tiring you out.
Zone 3 (brisk, approx. 70–80%): tempo run.
Zone 4–5 (hard, over 80%): intervals, only in short sections.
Formulas like “220 minus age” are only rough estimates and can be off by 10–15 beats. When in doubt, rely on feel and the talk test.
The most important rule
About 80% of your running time should be truly easy. Most runners run their easy runs too fast and their hard ones too slow – turn that around.
Warm-up & running drills
Ready for any session in 10 minutes.
Before every run
Jog very easily or walk briskly for 5–10 minutes. Your body warms up, heart rate and breathing rise slowly.
For easy runs that's enough: simply start the first few minutes deliberately slower.
Additionally before tempo runs, intervals and hill runs
Running drills (approx. 20–30 m each, 1–2 rounds): ankle drills (small, quick steps on the forefoot), high knees, butt kicks, skipping.
Then 3–4 strides over 60–80 m: start easy, build up to about 85% of top speed, ease off, walk back.
Static stretching (long holds) doesn't belong before hard sessions – move dynamically instead: leg swings, lunges, hip circles.
Cool-down
Jog easily or walk for 5–10 minutes until your heart rate and breathing have settled.
Afterwards is a good time for light stretching of calves, thighs and hips.
Running technique
Run efficiently and easy on the joints.
Posture
Upright, leaning slightly forward – from the ankles, not bending at the hips.
Look ahead (approx. 10–20 m), shoulders relaxed and low, hands loose, don't tense up.
Stride
Your foot should land under your centre of gravity, not far in front of you. Long strides landing on the heel in front of your body brake you and strain the knees.
A slightly higher cadence often helps: many short, light steps rather than a few long ones. A guideline for many runners: around 165–180 steps per minute – but it's individual.
Whether you land on your heel, midfoot or forefoot is secondary. What matters more is that your foot doesn't land far in front of your body.
Arms
Swing your arms loosely back and forth at about a 90-degree angle, not across your body.
Stronger arm movements help on hills and in the final sprint.
Breathing
Breathe through your mouth and nose, whatever feels natural.
Side stitch: slow down, breathe out deeply and slowly, walk briefly if needed.
Progress safely & prevent injuries
How to keep going without overdoing it.
Increase slowly
Only ever increase one thing: duration, frequency or pace – not everything at once.
Muscles and endurance adapt faster than tendons, ligaments and bones. Even if it feels easy: give your body time.
The recovery weeks in the plan are important – that's where progress is consolidated.
Warning signs
Normal: mild muscle soreness, tired legs the next day.
Pause and observe: pain that gets worse while running, sits in one specific spot (e.g. shin, heel, knee, top of the foot) or makes you limp.
See a doctor: pain that doesn't improve after a few days' rest, swelling, chest pain, dizziness or unusual shortness of breath.
What helps
Strength training 1–2× per week (legs, hips, core) makes you more stable – GainPilot's strength plans can be combined with running plans.
Sleep and eating enough are part of training.
Choose running shoes by feel: they should be comfortable and not pinch. Many runners replace them after about 600–1000 km.
Strength training and running on the same day
Try not to schedule hard runs and heavy leg days directly after each other.
If both have to be on the same day: the more important one first, with a few hours' break in between.
Eating & drinking around running
Energy for training and recovery.
Before
Short, easy runs also work on an empty stomach or after a small snack.
Before longer or hard sessions, have an easily digestible meal with carbohydrates 1–3 hours beforehand, e.g. oats, bread, banana. Little fat and fibre right before.
On the way
Under about 60 minutes, water is usually enough – or nothing at all.
On longer runs: drink regularly and take in carbohydrates from about 60–75 minutes (e.g. gel, banana, sports drink). Try it out in training, never for the first time on race day.
After
Within a few hours, a meal with protein and carbohydrates – that supports recovery.
Drink enough throughout the day, especially in the heat.
5 km test & race
Measure your progress and run well on the big day.
Warm up well (10 min easy plus 3 strides).
Run the 5 km as evenly as possible, holding back a little in the first half and picking it up at the end.
Log the run in GainPilot: it counts towards your running score on the leaderboard.
The last days before the race
The last week is calmer: less volume, a few short, brisk sections keep you fresh.
Don't try anything new: no new shoes, no unfamiliar food.
On race day
Arrive in good time and warm up easily.
Don't start too fast – the excitement makes you faster than planned. Stick to your target pace.
After the run: cool down, drink, eat and recover easily over the following days.
Easy base run
The foundation of every plan – easy and steady.
Goal
Builds aerobic endurance: heart, circulation and muscles become more efficient without you needing long recovery.
How it works
Start calmly and then stay steadily in the easy zone (RPE 2–4, talk test passed).
Walking breaks are explicitly allowed if your heart rate gets too high.
Common mistakes
Too fast: if the run feels like a “good workout”, it's usually too hard.
Wanting to set a personal best every time – that's what other sessions are for.
Long run
The longest session of the week – duration before pace.
Strengthens endurance, gets muscles, tendons and mind used to long efforts and improves fat metabolism.
Run at an easy pace, rather slower than your normal runs.
On runs over 60–75 minutes, take water and possibly carbohydrates with you.
A flat, varied route or a loop that passes a drinks stop makes it easier.
Starting too fast and fading at the end.
Scheduling the long run right after a hard day – better plan it after a rest day.
Recovery run
Short and very easy – helps recovery.
Stimulate blood flow and loosen the legs without adding a new training stimulus.
Very slow, shorter than your other runs, zone 1–2 or RPE 2–3.
Flat route, ideally on soft ground.
Good to know
If you feel tired or run-down, a rest day or a walk is the better choice.
The gentle start – alternating running and walking.
Build endurance without overdoing it. Ideal for getting started or returning after a break.
Run the given sections very easily and keep walking briskly during the breaks.
From week to week the running sections get longer and the walking breaks shorter.
An interval watch or a phone timer helps with switching.
If a week was too hard, repeat it – that's completely normal.
Run with strides
Easy run plus short, brisk sections.
Improves running technique, cadence and speed without tiring you out.
First do the easy run as planned.
Then 4–6 strides over approx. 60–100 m: start slowly, build up to about 85–90% of your top speed, ease off.
Between the strides, walk all the way back or jog easily until you feel fresh again.
Sprinting all out – the strides should feel smooth and relaxed.
Tempo run & tempo blocks
Brisk and controlled – pushes up your comfortable pace.
Raises the pace you can hold for a long time (threshold). Very effective for 5 km to half marathon.
Warm up for 10–15 minutes, running drills and 2–3 strides.
Run the tempo section briskly but under control (RPE 6–7, short sentences still possible). With tempo blocks, several sections with short jogging breaks.
In a progression run, start easy and raise the pace in stages; the last third is brisk.
Cool down for 10 minutes.
Starting too fast: the last kilometre should be just as fast as or faster than the first.
Tempo runs on two days in a row.
Interval training
Fast sections with breaks – for more speed and oxygen uptake.
Increases maximum oxygen uptake and speed. Short intervals (e.g. 400 m) make you faster, long ones (e.g. 1000 m) improve speed endurance.
Warm up thoroughly: 10–15 minutes easy, running drills, 3–4 strides.
Run the intervals hard but evenly (RPE 7–9). All repetitions should be about the same speed.
During the breaks, jog easily or walk as stated in the plan.
In pyramids the sections first get longer, then shorter again – pace yourself accordingly.
Running the first interval far too fast – better start a little conservatively and pick it up at the end.
Too little recovery between hard days: intervals are followed by at least one easy day.
A 400 m track or a measured route makes it easier; with a GPS watch it works anywhere.
Fartlek
Pace changes by feel and terrain.
Trains speed endurance and pace feel in a playful way – less rigid than intervals.
After warming up, alternate between fast and easy sections as the plan, terrain and your feel dictate: e.g. fast to the next lamp post, then easy to the crossroads.
Run the fast sections brisk to hard, and the easy ones truly easy.
Off-road you use hills and paths as natural sections.
Fartlek is ideal when you don't feel like watches and numbers.
Hill runs & hill intervals
Strength and speed on the slope.
Strengthens legs and feet, improves running economy and prepares you for hilly routes – with less impact than fast runs on the flat.
Find a steady incline (approx. 4–8% gradient).
After warming up, run up the hill sections powerfully: stay upright, short steps, active arm swing, eyes forward.
Jog or walk easily back down – that's the break.
For longer hill repeats, choose a pace at which the last repeat still goes just as well.
Leaning far forward.
Running downhill too fast – that puts a lot of strain on knees and thighs.
Trail & cross-country running
Running on forest tracks and paths.
Strengthens feet, ankles and coordination, adds variety and is gentle thanks to soft ground.
Run by time and effort, not pace – off-road you're automatically slower.
Walk steep climbs calmly; even pros do that.
Downhill, take short, quick steps and look a few metres ahead.
Safety
Check the route beforehand, take your phone and let someone know on longer runs.
Shoes with good grip help on slippery ground.
